title: The Reappearance by Aspiration Sutta
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Sankharupapatti Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 120), opening with a joke about Niels Bohr's good-luck horseshoe, which works whether or not anyone believes in it. In the sutta, a bhikkhu fixes the mind on rebirth among nobles and then among ever higher gods, until the last paragraph drops any future and enters deliverance here and now. Norman connects this to the Buddha's one more miracle, a thought arising and passing away, and to Dogen's death poem. Norman recalls doing Ayya Khema's funeral with Ajahn Amaro, one celebrating her freedom from rebirth, the other her return again and again. Norman closes with the practice of showing up when the bell rings, sitting, bowing, and answering yes when the Buddha calls.

sentences.text: Did you hear my joke about Niels Bohr, the scientist?
It's a good joke, I'll tell you my joke.
So, Niels Bohr has a horseshoe for good luck over the door to his house.
Somebody comes to visit him and they're surprised that Niels Bohr would have a horseshoe for good luck over the door of his house.
They say, "Niels, you can't possibly believe in good luck horseshoes, right?"
And Niels Bohr says, "Right, of course not.
Who could believe in such superstitious nonsense?
I mean, I'm quite aware of the many forces in the universe and luck is not one of them."
The person says, "Yeah, but why do you have that horseshoe over your door?"
And Niels Bohr said, "Well, someone told me that it works whether you believe in it or not."
It's a pretty good joke, right?
This reminds me of our practice, which also works whether you believe in it or not.
I think it's better not to believe in it, or anyway, if you can't help yourself, but believe in it, not to believe in it too much, because you might forget that there's nothing to believe in.
You would be better off to be like Niels Bohr, a materialist in a material world.
In Western thought, all the way back to the Greeks, there has always been a great division between the material world and the spiritual world.
For a long time, up until maybe the last couple of hundred years, people believed that the material world was a thin veil covering the spiritual world, which was the really real world.
But now we don't believe in that anymore.
We believe, absolutely believe in the material world, which we know for sure is really, really real, and that the spiritual world doesn't exist at all.
It's just something that foolish people in the past who didn't know any better were brainwashed to believe in superstitiously, like a good luck horseshoe.
And now we know better.
In Buddhism, actually, the idea is that neither one of these worlds really exists, neither the material world nor the spiritual world.
In any way, they might as well be the same thing.
They are the same thing, which is what we learned more or less yesterday from Suzuki Roshi.
Bohr would probably appreciate this a lot because, as you know, he was the great originator of quantum thought, or one of the originators of quantum thought.

I think I usually get this wrong, but I think it's more or less anyway true that he invented the concepts of complementarity and entanglement, the quantum concepts of complementarity and entanglement.
Complementarity describes, among other things, the fact that light, when you examine it one way, is particles, and when you examine it another way, it's waves.
So that's weird.
Light is a wave, light is a particle, but a particle is not a wave, and a wave is not a particle.
So is light a wave or a particle or neither or both?
Entanglement describes the bizarre fact that particles extremely distant from one another can have simultaneous mutual influence, even though there's no discernible causal connection between them.
So Niels Bohr was a materialist who understood that the material world isn't exactly the material world as we perceive and understand it.
This whole business to me illustrates the eternal principle that the more you know, the less you can be sure of, which is, I guess, more or less the uncertainty principle.

You realize that your knowledge can't ever be objective or completely accurate because in the moment that you are seeking and producing knowledge, your seeking itself and the object of your knowing have already shifted.
In a world of nervous people craving certainty, this is bad news, especially bad news for knowledgeable people.
And yet, just like the joke says, we heard that knowledge works even though you can't really believe in it.
I think we can have a great sympathy for all the people who talk about fake news and fake science.
They're right, although they seem to draw the wrong conclusions, they're right.
Anyway, that's not what I want to talk about this morning.
I just had that on my mind for a minute.

What I would like to talk about this morning is a short sutta from the Pali Canon called the Sankhya Rupa Patti Sutta, which Bhikkhu Bodhi translates that title as the Reappearance by Aspirations Sutta.
It's number 120 in the Majjhima Nikaya, the middle length discourses.
So I'll read to you from the beginning of the sutta.
*Thus have I heard on one occasion the Blessed One was living at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove in Adapindika's Park.*
You know the story of Adapindika, right, who was a great lay disciple of the Buddha and a great friend of Shariputra especially.
There's a wonderful sutta of Shariputra in speaking to Adapindika on his deathbed.
It's a very profound sutta.
But Adapindika donated this big piece of land to the Buddha.

And the prince, Jeta, who was sort of the boss of the area, when he found out about this, he was a little jealous, that Adapindika had given the Buddha this land and he wanted to give the Buddha something.
He said, "Well, let me buy the land from you so I can give it to the Buddha."
And Adapindika said, "No, no, I'm giving it to the Buddha."
So Prince Jeta kept begging him.
And Adapindika said, "Well, all right, I'll tell you what."
*As much land as you can cover with gold coins, that much land I'll give you and you can give it to the Buddha.*
Adapindika thought that this was like a ridiculous thing.
In other words, no, but he said it that way.
So Prince Jeta actually did this.
He went out and got gold and he filled up the entire place with gold.
And Adapindika said, "Well, OK."
So that was Jeta's grove in Adapindika's park, and that's where the Buddha was at this time.
And the Buddha then in that place, and it was a place where the Buddha went a lot.
He was appearing in Savatthi a lot on his travels.
So he said there to the Bhikkhus, "Bhikkhus."
And they said, "Venerable Sir, as I always tell you, if this were a Zen sutta, it would end there.
That would be the whole thing.
That would be the whole thing, because that would be all that would be necessary for the Buddhas to say Bhikkhus and for the Bhikkhus to say yes."
A lot of Zen stories are exactly that.
You've heard Zen stories exactly like that, because that's all you need.
All you need is a call and a response, a human call, a human response.
Whatever the content is, it hardly matters.
When the call is clear and the response is from the heart, that's all you need.
But this is not a Zen story.
This is a Pali sutta, so the Buddha will go on at some length.
So he said, because he needs to say first "Bhikkhus," and they need to say yes, because he's sort of saying, "Are you ready to listen?"
Maybe they're not.
If they didn't say yes, he'd say, "Well, OK, no use speaking."
But they're ready to listen, so he teaches them.
*Bhikkhus, I shall teach you reappearance in accordance with one's aspirations.
Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.*
"Yes, venerable sir," the Bhikkhus replied.
So the word here translated as aspiration is Sankara, the word in the title of the sutra, which is samskara in Sanskrit.
It's usually translated as impulse or formation.
Sometimes it could be translated as intention.
It's one of the five skandhas, the five constituents of self.
It more or less means our desire or our life force, our drive toward a future.
It's a force that is a basic human drive in us and something that the Buddha thought about a lot since it leads us to so much suffering.
But here, I think it's fair to translate it as aspiration, as you'll see from the context.
So aspiration for reappearance, and reappearance means rebirth.
And as we'll see in a minute, the Buddha is talking about the aspiration, the drive, the desire to achieve a favorable rebirth after this life is over.
So the Blessed One said this.
*Here, Bhikkhus, a Bhikkhu possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
He thinks, oh, that on the dissolution of the body after death, I might reappear in the company of well-to-do nobles.
He fixes his mind on that, establishes it, and develops it.
These aspirations and this abiding of his, thus developed and cultivated, leads to his reappearance there.
This, Bhikkhus, is the path, the way that leads to reappearance there.*

Again, a Bhikkhu possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and thinks, "Oh, that on the dissolution of the body after death, I might reappear in the company of well-to-do Brahmins, in the company of well-to-do householders."
And he fixes his mind on that.
And this, Bhikkhus, is the path, the way that leads to reappearance there.
He's repeating all these allusions.
The same thing is repeated over and over and over again in all of its particulars, but I'm leaving that out, the repetition, just like Bhikkhu Bodhi does in his translation.
Again, a Bhikkhu possesses faith, and so forth and so on.
And here is that the gods of the heaven of the four great kings are long live, beautiful, and enjoy great happiness.
He says that on the dissolution of the body after death, I might reappear in the company of the gods of the heaven of the four great kings.
And he fixes his mind on that.
And then he will reappear in that realm because of his aspiration.
This Bhikkhus is the path, the way that leads to reappearance there.

So in other words, if you have an aspiration to be born in a wonderful realm that you can think about, and you are a person who practices diligently and wise and you have faith and so on and so on, and you fix your mind on that, you actually can be reborn there.

So the Bhikkhu is telling them that if they are virtuous and generous and diligent and they think about a future life that they would like to have and they think about it strong enough, they will actually be reborn there.
Their aspiration will work.
They will be reborn in that wonderful state.

This is just like some preachers you hear on the radio or TV who say, "If you want to be rich and have a big car, all you have to do is set your aspiration on that and pray to the Lord and you will get it.
So if you send money to me, that will also be good.
But you'll get this."
This is not just limited to Christian evangelicals.
There are also some Buddhists who chant the name of the Lotus Sutra like we mentioned the other day, so as to develop their intention to be rich and successful.
And then thanks to this developed intention and with the help of the Buddha, this will come about.
But you don't even need to be religious to have this kind of thing going on.
The self-help teachers also preach this very thing.
They say "Follow your bliss and the money will come."
They say, "Just set your heart on what you really, really want and if you want it enough and if you're diligent enough in that aspiration, you will get it."
So it appears that they all got this from the Buddha was preaching pretty much this same thing two thousand five hundred years ago before there was even a Jesus or a self-help.
So he mentions in the part I read so far, first of all being born into a noble family and then being born into a Brahmin family and then being born into the first of the God realms.
So this is a hierarchy.
Every paragraph repeats exactly the same thing only with the next higher possible rebirth.
And it goes on for quite a while and each successive paragraph proposes an aspiration for a realm higher than the last.
And it goes on and on and on and on.
Do you have water or something there?
Because you could have this tea.
Why don't you go give her that?
So I'll just give you a couple a little bit further.
Again, a bhikkhu possesses faith, et cetera, et cetera, and hears about the gods of the heaven of the thirty-three, which is the next highest heaven.
He hears about et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
Next one, he hears about the gods in the Tushita heaven.
The next one, he hears about the gods who delight in creating.
The next highest one, the gods who wield power over others' creations.
So these gods who create, but then the gods who direct the creation of others.
And there, there's a fabulous realm over there because they live a really long life and everything is beautiful.

Plus, they get to direct, not only recreate it themselves, but to direct, it's like Damien Hirst or something, who has six hundred artists working in his studio, and he just tells them what to make the art, and then they pay him.
It's a great thing.
He's like one of those gods in that realm.
And if they fix their mind on this, they will reappear there, and it goes on.
Then, what about the Brahma of a thousand?

The Brahma of a thousand is a long life, beautiful, and he's very happy, and he abides intent on pervading a world system in which there's not only one world in which you can direct everybody's creation, but there's a thousand worlds.
A thousand worlds, like universes like this one, in which you could be a god directing everybody's creation.
And he has an aspiration to be reborn there, and he is.

And the Buddha says, just as a man with good sight might take a gall nut—I'm not sure exactly what a gall nut is—but a gall nut in his hand and review it, look at it, so the Brahma of a thousand abides intent on pervading a world system of a thousand worlds and abides intent on pervading the beings that have reappeared there.
So every one of the beings in these five world systems is pervaded by the spirit of this Brahma.
Wow, what a world.
The Bhikkhu says, "Wow, yes, on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might reappear in that Brahma world."
And if he fixes his mind on that, he will.
And this, Bhikkhu, is the path, the way that leads to reappearance there.
But then it goes on further: two thousand.
Why only one thousand?
Two thousand.
Four thousand.
Five thousand.
It's like he has five gall nuts in his hand, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
I will skip the rest, but it goes on for quite a while.
So this is good news for those of us with aspirations for the future.
We can realize our aspirations.
All we have to do is practice faith, wisdom, and virtue, be virtuous and really develop our aspiration, and it will work out.
By now, I think Tim said this also the other day, by now you're getting the idea that this is a setup.
The other shoe will be dropping soon.
The Buddha is going to, like, deflate this whole thing.
And he does.
Here's the last paragraph of the sutta.
Again, Bhikkhu possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, just like in all the other cases.

And he thinks, "Oh, by realizing for myself with direct knowledge, I might hear and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and the deliverance by wisdom that are taintless and with the destruction of taints."
And by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, he hears and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and the deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of taints.
Bhikkhus, this Bhikkhu does not reappear anywhere at all.
This is what the Blessed One said, and the Bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words.

So this reminds me of a sutta that we read in our Dharma seminar at home a month or so ago in which the Buddha comes out of his room and goes into the monk's room and they're chatting about the miracles that were attendant on the Buddha's birth.

And then the Buddha asks Mahamogalyana, who knows a lot about this, to talk to the monastics about all the miracles that were attendant on the Buddha's birth and Mahamogalyana in a very similar way tells a whole bunch of miracles, each one more spectacular than the last.
And when he gets finished with all these miracles, the Buddha says, "Well, there's one more miracle.
Do you want me to tell you one more miracle?"
And they say, "Yeah."
And he says, "Well, this great miracle is that an awakened person can have a thought or a feeling or a perception, and she can appreciate it as it arises, as it abides, and as it passes away.
Isn't that a great Buddha miracle?"
So this is a very Zen-like teaching.
What is the greatest miracle of all?
A thought in your mind, rising, abiding, passing away.
Even a thought you don't like, arising, abiding, passing away.
There's a passage by Dogen called Miracles.

And I'm pretty sure I spoke about this at one session here, maybe even last year, in which Dogen shows the great miracle of a teacher waking up from a nap, and the disciple offers him a damp towel so he can wash his face.
Anyway, back to our present text, which actually, when you think about it, is very important.
Because Buddha seems to be saying in his way, very indirectly, that there is always something painful in our aspiration, our desire for a future state, even when it works out.
Even when we realize that wonderful future state, and we really are reborn into that future state.
Sometimes we say, "Well, don't be so passionate about what you want in the future.
Probably it won't work out anyway.
Just be present."
But here the Buddha says, "Oh yes, actually it will work out.
If you want it enough, and if your practice is diligent, it will work out.
You will get what you want.
Later, anyway, after you die, you'll get it, in this case."
But the question is, is it really worthwhile to be born in the realm of the gods of the five thousand?
The final paragraph in which the Buddha expresses what we assume to be his preferred view really doesn't have any aspiration in it at all.
And it has no future in it at all.
There's no rebirth whatsoever.

"Oh, that by realizing for myself with direct knowledge, I might hear and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints."
That seems to be what the Buddha is proposing as the alternative.
Now, to be sure, this hypothetical Bhikkhu who's saying this says, "I might," which maybe sounds a little bit like a projection into a future, but then he says, "I might hear and now."

So this might isn't so much an aspiration for a future as it is a determination, a kind of intervention or interruption, that right now I will stop whatever else I might wish or long for and enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind, meaning right now I will liberate my mind.

I will not wait for a future wonderful moment in which I will liberate my mind, but now, right now I will liberate my mind, clarify my mind, be completely with my mind as it is right now, and I will be delivered by wisdom that is pure, meaning wisdom that is beyond any idea of purity or impurity or any projection of what we think wisdom looks like, but wisdom that is just the wisdom that is here now, seeing things as they are, however pleasant or unpleasant they may appear to be.
And if he will do this, the Buddha says, this Bhikkhu will not reappear anywhere at all.
He will have nothing in his hands.
She will only be fully alive right here.
She will disappear into this moment.
And then at the time of her death, she will completely disappear, like we were saying yesterday, completely leap into the arms of what cannot be known beyond all limitation and conception.
Dogen's great death poem: *For 53 years I've hung the sky with stars.
Now I leap through.* What a shattering.
So in terms of the Sutta, they're speaking about rebirth.
But I'm sure that it refers to more than rebirth.
And rebirth is more than rebirth.
Remember, this is a teaching about samskaras, aspirations, desires, the drive to survive and flourish and have a wonderful time.

Buddha is saying that no matter how pure and wonderful an aspiration is, no matter how exalted and spiritual its object is, as long as it is a pressure toward a future state by its nature, it leaps over the present moment, which is the only moment in which direct knowledge is possible.
Direct knowledge in the present moment, knowledge born of wisdom without taints, is more than just be here now and forget the past and forget the future.
Direct knowledge is not knowing something.
Knowing something is always indirect knowledge.
There is the knower and the known object.
It is indirect, always.
Direct knowledge means no knower, no object of knowledge, no knowing, the emptiness of the three wheels.
Direct knowledge is not knowing.
It is seeing the vastness of our lives right here where we are in whatever state of mind we're in.
Direct knowledge is disappearing into your life.
Direct knowledge is asking all the time whether you have these words or not.
What is it?
And answering all the time whether you have these words or not.
This is it.
Direct knowledge is being willing to respond, yes sir, when the Buddha calls.
Even though you don't know what to do or say, you respond anyway.
Direct knowledge is continuing with your practice ever and ever, no matter what happens.
I am sure that some of you have heard me tell the story of Ayah Kama's funeral.
By now, everybody's heard all my stories, you know, at least once.
So some of you have heard me tell the story of Ayah Kama's funeral.
For those of you who don't know, Ayah was a great person and a very, very dear teacher for me.
She reminded me of my grandmother.
She was a really little woman, as my grandmother was.
She came for years.
She came on an annual visit to Gringalch, and she would give a retreat.
And I had such a great time going to her retreats and hanging out with her and getting to know her.
We had a wonderful communication and relationship.

And she was a very feisty little Jewish lady who had fled Nazi Germany as a child and somehow ended up in Shanghai because there was a small group of Jewish refugees who were not accepted to any European country.
You know, they kept being turned away.
Some of them ended up going back to Germany, but somehow Ayah and her family ended up in Shanghai, which is how she first became enamored of the East and of Buddhism.
She got married.
She had a family.
She traveled all around the world in a VW bus, like people did in those days.
And I think she ended up in San Diego.
But when I knew her, she was a noble Theravadan nun, and an extremely powerful meditator and a very, very tough teacher, no-nonsense teacher, who couldn't be bothered with anybody's problems.
You just go for the meditation, you know.
It was really something.
So when she died, Ajahn Amaro and I did her funeral at Gringalch.
And at that time, Amaro and I were very close friends.
And sadly, he's moved to England, you know, years ago, and I never see him anymore.
But when I was thinking about this this morning, I thought, why don't I go see him?
Why don't I go to England and see him?
I haven't seen him in quite a while.
Anyway, so we were doing the funeral, and Ajahn Amaro got up and said, "Oh, Ayah, we love you, and we are so happy that now you are beyond rebirth in this sad world.
Finally, you are pure, and you have completely gone beyond all this."

And I got up and I said, "Oh, Ayah, we love you, and we're so happy that you are traveling on and on, birth after birth after birth, in the six realms, for the benefit of sentient beings, and we're thrilled that we're going to see you again and again and again."
So Amaro and I were saying exactly the same thing.
In the particular languages of our respective traditions.
As we all know in Mahayana Buddhism, the Buddhism of the Bodhisattva, practice goes on and on forever, or at least until we fulfill our vow to save the infinite number of sentient beings.
But it is practice that goes on, not born from our samskaras, not born of our aspirations and desire for a future self.
It is practice that just goes on and on and on, on its own.
And forever is not a future.
Forever is now.
And now doesn't exist.
It's empty of time and space.
Disappearing even as it appears.
And in just this way, it goes on forever.
Being born and dying, not out of a desire or a fear, but out of love.
I really think that this is what the Buddha was getting at in this sutta.
This is how we would read it from a Mahayana perspective.
Awakening is not a better experience later.
That's suffering.
Awakening is nothing at all.
So this is what we are trying to do.
This is what we are trying to understand.
But how could you do this?
How?
If you can't really do it and you can't even have aspiration and desire to do it, how would you do it?
Could you ever really get rid of aspiration and desire for a future self?
No.
I don't think you can get rid of it.
But I think you can transmute it.

Instead of desiring a future state, liberation, enlightenment, religious experience, rebirth in higher realms, you can practice your desire and aspiration right now by letting go on every moment you can.
And just practice right here and now.
Practice is never later.
It's only ever right here and now.
Interrupt yourself.
Take a breath.
Return to zero in the body.
Dogen calls this continuous practice.
The aspiration, the desire, becomes the aspiration and the desire to practice forever for the benefit of all beings.
Forever is now.
All beings are right here in your body, in your mind.
So we all know the method for effecting this transformation, this transmutation.
We all know how to do it.
Show up when the bell rings.
Sit down.
When the bell rings, get up.
Bow.
Chant.
Put on the robe, take off the robe.
Walk.
Eat.
Sleep.
Practice kindness with everyone you meet.

Practice trust with your teacher so your life can be transformed by trust and you can accept whatever this moment brings, whatever the Buddha calls you to, you can say yes, and you can trust yourself to know how to practice with whatever this present moment will bring.
You just walk the path one step at a time, step by step, every step complete, full.
Appreciate your hopes and dreams, your desperation, your anger, your sorrow, your pain.
You have been given these gifts for a reason.
So thank you very much for listening to my talk this morning.
Our intention equal extent.
